analysis.one_liner: Lets the SEC seek civil penalties for securities fraud up to ten years after a violation.
analysis.headline: A bill letting the SEC bring civil fraud penalty cases up to 10 years after a violation — double the general five-year limit — was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: After a Supreme Court ruling that the five-year clock for SEC civil penalties starts when the violation happens, not when the fraud is discovered, long-running frauds could escape penalties entirely. This bill would give the SEC ten years to bring a civil penalty case for a securities violation, and would pause that clock whenever the accused is outside the United States or has no fixed home or workplace in the country. It went to the Senate Banking Committee and never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiary would be the Securities and Exchange Commission, which could reach financial misconduct that surfaces late. Investors and retirement savers would benefit indirectly: a longer enforcement window means long-running frauds like Ponzi schemes and accounting cover-ups can still carry civil penalties, which deters misconduct and helps keep the market honest. Honest financial firms would also face competitors operating under a stronger deterrence regime.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The SEC, investors, and retirement savers

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives the SEC a ten-year window to seek civil monetary penalties for securities violations, up from the five-year limit that generally applies to civil penalties, so long-running schemes that surface late can still be penalized.

It pauses the clock whenever an alleged violator is absent from the United States or has no reasonably ascertainable home or workplace in the country, preventing wrongdoers from simply waiting out the deadline from abroad.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the cost would fall on securities firms, investment advisers, and individuals accused of violations, who would remain exposed to SEC civil penalty actions for up to a decade instead of five years — and even longer if they spend time abroad, since the clock pauses while they are outside the country. Some of that cost could be passed to clients through compliance and legal expenses.
analysis.who_pays_short: Securities firms and executives facing SEC penalties

drawbacks.text: Doubling the window from the general five-year limit to ten years means individuals and firms can face SEC civil penalty cases for conduct up to a decade old, when records and witnesses may be gone — a real cost to defendants' interest in finality.

The bill's tolling rule pauses the ten-year clock whenever an alleged violator is outside the United States or has no fixed home or workplace here, which in some cases could stretch the exposure period well beyond a decade.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but indirect: a longer enforcement window means securities fraud that comes to light late — exactly the pattern in complex financial schemes — can still draw civil penalties, which deters misconduct and helps keep markets honest for savers and investors. The cost falls on financial firms and individuals, who lose the certainty of knowing that conduct more than five years old is beyond the SEC's reach; records fade and memories dim, and the tolling rule for people outside the country could stretch exposure even further. On balance the bill modestly favors accountability over finality, but it is a targeted enforcement tweak, not a sweeping fix, and it was never seriously pursued.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced by Senator Reed and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it, and the two-year Congress ended without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed (D-RI) introduced the bill on September 18, 2014, joined by four Democratic colleagues — Levin, Markey, Shaheen, and Warren.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day it was introduced.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 113th Congress, which ended January 3, 2015.
Under current law, the general statute of limitations for civil penalties is five years, so the bill would have doubled the SEC's enforcement window to ten.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Securities firms and financial executives are better off, because the five-year limit on SEC penalty cases stands and old misconduct stays out of reach.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms facing SEC penalty exposure

for.name: Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Carl Levin, Ed Markey, Jeanne Shaheen, and Elizabeth Warren

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred — no hearing, no markup, no vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only five Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill and no vote ever occurred, so no partisan split can be measured; the bill simply sat in a committee whose members never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill doubles, to ten years, how long they remain exposed to SEC civil penalty actions for securities violations, and can extend that further for violators who spend time abroad. Longer legal exposure means more settlements and penalties over long-running schemes.

The bill's penalty provisions reach misconduct under the Investment Company and Investment Advisers Acts, so advisers and fund operators face the same ten-year exposure. The same rules protect the fund investors who are their customers.
